planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Foster is self-fruitful and does not need a pollinizer, but give it the same generous 20-25 foot mature spread as other full-size grapefruit.

directions: Plant grafted trees in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and mulch to conserve moisture through the long Gulf Coast summer. Foster arose in Florida in the early 1900s as a limb sport on a Walters grapefruit tree, making it one of the earliest pink-fleshed grapefruit ever found and a direct ancestor in the pigmented-grapefruit lineage that later produced Thompson, Ruby Red, and Star Ruby. Its flesh coloring is lighter and less consistent than those later red-fleshed selections, and the fruit still carries a modest number of seeds, but the tree is vigorous, cold-tolerant for a grapefruit, and appeals to gardeners who want a piece of citrus history rather than a modern seedless hybrid. Fruit matures in winter and, like most grapefruit, holds well on the tree and sweetens the longer it hangs.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Midknight Valencia Orange (Nearly Seedless Late-Season Sweet Orange)

planting.note: Plant container citrus in spring after cold risk passes, in the warmest, most frost-protected spot available; Midknight needs the same 3-5 years to reach significant bearing as standard Valencia.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate, feeding with a citrus fertilizer program three times a year as with any Valencia-type orange. Midknight is a bud sport of Valencia that originated in South Africa and was selected specifically because it produces far fewer seeds, typically none to a handful per fruit, while keeping the deep orange color, abundant juice, and classic sweet-tart Valencia flavor. Like standard Valencia, it ripens uniquely late in the season, holding on the tree from spring into early summer after navels and other oranges have finished, which makes it a good way to stretch home dooryard citrus harvest into the hottest months. It shares Valencia's relatively good cold tolerance for a sweet orange, tolerating brief dips into the mid-20s F once established.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Sanguinelli Blood Orange (Spanish Seedless Blood Orange)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sanguinelli colors up more reliably than Moro in areas with mild winter nights, which makes it a better bet for many Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and water deeply and regularly through summer while fruit sizes up. Sanguinelli arose in Spain in the late 1920s as a bud mutation of the older Doblefina blood orange and is valued for being essentially seedless while still developing the streaked red rind and red-mottled flesh characteristic of blood oranges. Its pigmentation is more moderate and more dependable in warm-winter climates than the deeply colored Moro, since Sanguinelli does not require as many cold nights to color well, and its flavor carries a milder raspberry-like note over a standard sweet-orange base. Fruit ripens mid-season in winter and has a notably thin, smooth rind that peels easily for fresh eating.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
